entries.title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup
entries.summary: Alfa by Lilja Sigurծardóttir; The Lost Spectacular by Zoé Duhaime; Look What the Cat Dragged In by Jason Rekulak; China +100: Stories from a Century After the Outbreak edited by Xueting C Ni; Everything Happens So Much by Andrew H MurrayAlfa by Lilja Sigurծardóttir, translated by Larissa Kyzer (Orenda, £10.99) The first speculative fiction by the Icelandic crime writer is set 26 years from now, wi
entries.content:
Alfa by Lilja Sigurծardóttir, translated by Larissa Kyzer (Orenda, £10.99)

The first speculative fiction by the Icelandic crime writer is set 26 years from now, with European countries united under the benevolent “omniocratic” rule of the titular artificial intelligence in Reykjavik. Universal basic income, autonomous vehicles and constant surveillance steering citizens towards their best lives are welcomed by most Icelanders, where only a few dissidents insist on living off-grid. When one of them is found murdered in a way that should have been impossible, questions are raised about the supposedly perfect system, creating fractures in the victim’s family – one of whom helped to establish the ruling AI, and still works closely with it. A fascinating, thoughtful, suspenseful tale grounded in believable characters, this could hardly be more timely.

The Lost Spectacular by Zoé Duhaime (Solaris, £18.99)

At the core of this debut is a Danish folk tale about Lukǿje, a Sandman-like character who knows more stories than anyone in the world. Set in a “City Not-Unlike-Montréal” and another that could almost be New York, it follows the careers of two former best friends, now enemies. Munro envies Noon’s magical ability to jump into different places and times through books or pictures, and has never forgiven her for inheriting the bookshop he thought should have been his. In his role as a museum curator, Munro has developed a stalkerish method by which he tracks down and eliminates every access Noon could have into the worlds of her favourite stories. A fantastical literary battle unfolds. Whimsical with a dark edge, this bookish fantasy could develop a cult following.

Look What the Cat Dragged In by Jason Rekulak with illustrations by Doogie Horner and Will Staehle (Sphere, £22)

The second illustrated horror novel from the author of Hidden Pictures features Penny, creator of a popular series of comic books inspired by life with her cat, Popcorn. After Popcorn goes missing during a blizzard, Penny is grief-stricken and spirals into depression. When she’s convinced to foster another cat, Godfrey, she is comforted enough to make progress on her new book. But strange and unpleasant things are happening around her, and the panels she compulsively works on don’t look like her usual work – they frighten her. Echoes of Rosemary’s Baby hint at the danger threatening Penny. The illustrations are equally well done, adding another dimension to this very enjoyable spooky chiller.

China +100: Stories from a Century after the Outbreak edited by Xueting C Ni, various Chinese authors and translators (Comma, £11.99)

Eleven Chinese writers imagine a version of their country 100 years after the first outbreak of Covid-19. While the threat of another novel virus features in a few stories, most concentrate on how new inventions and discoveries, along with climate change, could alter the way people live. I Want a Different World by Zhou Dedong, one of China’s most famous horror writers, brings the China of 2019 into direct contact with 2119 as researchers in the future use a new invention capable of capturing data from traces of body heat left in the past. They are attempting to solve the mystery of how a man named Xu Zhi managed to disappear from his Shanghai apartment in the early days of lockdown, never to be seen again. A compelling tale with unexpected twists, it packs a strong emotional punch as we learn of Xu Zhi’s desperate attempts to reach his wife, confined in hospital. Many things will undoubtedly change in 100 years, but some, like the anguish of being separated from loved ones, won’t. A fine batch of diverse stories, and an opportunity to read SF from a Chinese perspective.

Everything Happens So Much by Andrew H Murray (Orion, £18.99)

In a world very like our own, the existence of alternate universes has been monetised with the invention of a drug that allows the consumer to observe an alternate existence from behind the eyes of an alternate self – usually a happier, richer, more successful one. Esme Good, stuck in a boring job, has become addicted to these second-hand experiences, until one day everything changes. Suddenly Esme has become the most important person in her universe, and unless she finds a way to get her boring old life back, it could mean the end of her world. A confusing, fitfully amusing, snarky comic fantasy with touches of surrealism (there’s a talking leg), somewhat in the vein of Douglas Adams.

entries.title: ‘We are dream-walking into a desperate situation’: the Booker prize winner on his sci-fi alien invasion wakeup call
entries.summary: He is a sci-fi titan but M John Harrison has just exploded into the mainstream – with The End of Everything, an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast. Does he really think we have no hope left?With his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Bo
entries.content:
With his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Booker prize for fiction, for his 13th novel, The End of Everything. Our interview is delayed because of wifi issues, which is fitting given that the novel is about – among many things – what happens when non-human intelligence takes over.

The End of Everything is the first sci-fi novel to have won the prize in its 58-year history, which is almost as long as Harrison has been writing. “It’s interesting,” he replies, when asked if he feels vindicated, “that something that has an SF-adjacent feel can be regarded as a serious book and given the Booker prize. My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre. I don’t believe in it in any way.” He gently wags his finger at me. It is a bit like having coffee with a cheerier, more neatly bearded Gandalf – it will surprise no one that, in his youth, Harrison read The Lord of the Rings every year for a decade.

Whether he likes it or not, Harrison is hailed as a titan of literary science fiction. His fans have included giants such as the late Ursula K Le Guin and Iain Banks, as well as China Miéville today, and more surprisingly the Sex and the City star, and last year’s Booker judge, Sarah Jessica Parker. But he is not, as he would be the first to say, a household name. Although that has been changing. In 2020 he won the Goldsmiths prize for The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again, and in 2022 he was himself a Booker judge.

The End of Everything took around 15 years to write, with real-world events overtaking him. AI, late capitalism, environmental collapse, the refugee crisis, Brexit – nearly all the manifestations of today’s omni-crisis can be found in the pages of this slim, elusive novel. As its title suggests, this is the work for our end times. “I suddenly thought, ‘Well, you’re 80, you might as well have a go at pushing it over the cliff one more time.’ My rule has always been push it as far as it will go, then move back slightly from the edge. But this time I thought, ‘Let’s push it over and see what happens.’”

And what happens is anyone’s guess. As critics have pointed out, The End of Everything deliberately resists definition. It is a triumph of obfuscation. “I could explain some of it to you,” the author says tantalisingly. “But no, I don’t want to.” For Harrison, the world ends not with a bang, but with endless confusion. “It was a book designed to present the explanatory collapse and epistemological collapse that you see in societies that have suddenly lost their grounding.”

He describes it as a mix of gothic horror, road movie, science fiction and fantasy – even “a seaside novel”. I would add satire to the list. One thing it is not, Harrison is clear, is a dystopia, but rather a post-disaster novel in the tradition of early JG Ballard or John Wyndham. But he wanted to play with the conventions; he didn’t want the reader to know more than the characters. “It would be ordinary sci-fi,” he says, “if you were told it was the triffids.”

Set in an unnamed coastal town somewhere in Kent (“If this is hell, it looks a lot like Margate,” as Peaky Blinders famously had it) in the nearish future, The End of Everything depicts a disintegrating Britain, after an invasion by an alien species called the iGhettis, which appear as “tall writhing bursts of light”. The iGhettis are a play on “I get it” (explanation), “I get stuff” (capitalism), Getty (extreme wealth), Apple (tech), I (Freud). “I wrote it down and I thought, ‘This is cheap.’ And then I looked at it again and thought, ‘Oh my God, there are so many ambiguities packed into that one word,’” he says with glee.

The germ of the novel was the financial crisis of 2007-8. “I had the rage, but I couldn’t make it work.” So he put what he had written away in a drawer and in 2015 “cannibalised” it for a short story called The Crisis. It was almost the end of him. During a reading of the story at an event in east London, he was struck by what felt like the worst indigestion of his life. “I thought, ‘That’ll teach you to down two glasses of red wine and eat pizza before performing.’” Two days later he was taken to hospital and told he’d had a heart attack. He was just shy of 70. When he returned to The Crisis, he realised it was the blueprint for a whole novel. “I was like, ‘Wow!’ And began to work on it.”

Harrison was born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945. The closeness of the second world war overshadowed his childhood. “You were never allowed to forget it.” His father was an engineer, and the family lived on an estate of modern houses built for postwar key workers. One of the defining memories of his childhood was a Narnia-style wardrobe that, when he climbed into it, “was a library of trash novels” from 1920s thrillers to contemporary sci-fi magazines.

“It was full of all the things you weren’t supposed to enjoy,” he says with delight. He doesn’t know who the books belonged to. His parents had a very small bookcase with some classics downstairs in the lounge. “But it was the most extraordinary education for the imagination.” His father died when he was 13 and his mother never got over his death, something Harrison will explore if he ever writes his autobiography.

When he was 21, he published his first short story in the science-fiction magazine Science Fantasy. He became literary editor of New Worlds in 1968. He had a number of odd jobs – a groom at a hunting stables, a clerk, a trainee teacher. “Being a kind of hippy, I decided that if you were going to write, you would only write, and that you would take the consequences,” he says. That meant couch-surfing and often not having much to eat. “We were all living in appalling circumstances in west London before west London was west London,” he says of his fellow writers. “And it was great fun.”

Today he lives in rural Shropshire with his partner, the editor and writer Cath Phillips. He writes his first drafts in Moleskine notebooks, “always black and with squared paper” using Muji 0.5 pens, red and black. He is already working on an idea that may end up as a novel or short stories.

“Ever since I started in 1965,” he says, “my ambition has been to take down the divisions between genres. That’s been a guiding light.” As a reviewer for many years, he would ask: “Why should we be bad writers just because we’re writing science fiction? Why can’t we write good characters? Why shouldn’t we do it all?”

He is no longer angry with the publishing industry. “I’ve been mellowing as I age,” he says. He is now in his “late stage” as he calls it. “Older writers become knotty and gnarly. They just want to do what they want to do.” And this has worked. “I sold more books on the back of that position than I did by compromises with the industry.” And now he’s won its biggest prize.

The novel ends on what he calls “a positive” rather than a hopeful note. Does he feel hopeful for humanity? “No, I don’t feel any hope at all,” he replies bluntly. “We are just walking in a dream into a desperate situation. Somehow somebody has got to remind us that every action has consequences and that we’re ignoring them.”

Is that the responsibility of the novelist? “There are many,” he says. “To charm, to entertain. But I’ve always been Cassandra. It’s always a warning. ‘Be careful what you do.’”

  • The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Ten Lives by Mona Chalabi review – what if we were totally honest about our wealth?
entries.summary: The data journalist puts her own finances – and those of ten others from across the economic spectrum – under a microscopeHow much do you earn? If the question makes you bristle – and I realise we haven’t even met – would you answer it if someone convinced you that your candour might just change the world?In her deliciously original first book, the former Guardian data journalist and illustrator M
entries.content:
How much do you earn? If the question makes you bristle – and I realise we haven’t even met – would you answer it if someone convinced you that your candour might just change the world?

In her deliciously original first book, the former Guardian data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi sets out to do precisely that. The result – a dazzling mix of journalism, data visualisation and memoir – is both a joy to read and a serious provocation. Chalabi takes aim at our silence and furtiveness around individual income and finances. “Our collective ignorance is sustaining an unfair system,” she argues. Unless we talk more openly about our personal wealth, we will never be able to tackle the economic problems causing insecurity and anxiety for us all.

Ten Lives is a riveting exemplar of financial transparency. It tells the stories of 10 individual Americans, exploring how their wealth – or lack of it – has shaped every aspect of their lives. There is Jacob, the New York investment banker earning more than half a million dollars a year who uses an elastic band as a wallet, for fear of squandering money. There is former teen gambling addict Levi, now trying to rebuild his life in his 20s, whose greatest concern about being interviewed is the shame of appearing broke. There is grad student Kristina, newly divorced and forced to choose between finishing her degree and raising her child. Her solution is surrogacy. Being paid to grow someone else’s baby is the only way she can expand her options for childcare and, as a result, for her life.

Chalabi chose her subjects, whom she followed closely over a five-year period, to represent us all. In her introduction, she asks us to imagine lining up every person in the US from the poorest to the richest, then dividing that line into 10 equally sized groups. Each interviewee comes from one of those groups, or deciles, meaning all 10 steps on the US income ladder are depicted. Jacob is 10th decile (household income more than $272,000), Kristina is fifth ($59,000–$75,000) and Levi is third ($35,000–$46,000).

And then there is the 11th subject: Chalabi herself. Leading by example, she reveals the size of her advance for this book ($850,000 – or, in her terms, a “shitload of money”), provides a spreadsheet of her freelance earnings for the same five-year period as her subjects, and admits to having been able to buy a five-bedroom home in London for more than £1.5m. Her candour extends to revealing her discomfort as an advocate for social justice who has become, undeniably, rich. “If we rise too far, there’s a risk we will become the very thing we have criticised,” she admits.

Frankness is Chalabi’s signature trait. The words and illustrations that make up this book are an exhilarating antidote to obfuscation and evasiveness of every kind. She loathes all “word smush” that disguises reality, and her own prose is succinct, blunt and sinewy. Take, for example, her withering criticism of George Orwell for conducting a narcissistic poverty safari with Down and Out in Paris and London. The book is an example, she believes, of “class cosplay”, written by “a rich boy who changed his clothing and, presumably, his accent, to pass as a ‘tramp’”.

Considering its bedrock is hard numerical data, Ten Lives is a deeply affecting book. Her subjects’ stories reveal how easily systemic problems such as lack of affordable healthcare or childcare can overturn lives in modern America. Chalabi herself has to pour her savings into paying for care for her mother after she suffers a debilitating stroke in the UK. What unites all 11 of them is a gnawing fear for their financial futures – irrespective of how much they earn. The corrosive individualism of advanced capitalism supercharges these fears, argues Chalabi, by indoctrinating us into a belief that “we cannot support one another or be supported when we need to be.” But this is patently untrue. The world is not entirely dog-eat-dog. We can and do lean on family, friends and communities when we need to. We help each other out because we are care – and we are far from driven by avarice alone.

Chalabi concludes that what is needed to feel financially secure – and therefore to free ourselves from the treadmill of acquisition – is a proper societal safety net. A well-funded government, in other words, that spends enough on healthcare, education and welfare. To get there, instead of railing impotently at Bezos and Musk and the rest of the ultra-rich elite, we could start by being more open about how much wealth we have – and how much we owe and rely on each other. Otherwise, we will all remain in the dark, unsure, unprotected, afraid. It’s a brilliant, radical argument, delivered with ingenuity and panache.

entries.title: The Man With Many Names by Georgi Gospodinov review – playful and profound tales from Bulgaria
entries.summary: This collection of 40 short stories from the International Booker winner is full of invention and warmthIn the titular story of Georgi Gospodinov’s short-story collection The Man With Many Names, the narrator reveals: “Telling our personal stories is the only move we can make … that allows us to postpone for at least a little while this game’s foregone ending.” It’s as good a description as any of
entries.content:
In the titular story of Georgi Gospodinov’s short-story collection The Man With Many Names, the narrator reveals: “Telling our personal stories is the only move we can make … that allows us to postpone for at least a little while this game’s foregone ending.” It’s as good a description as any of the Bulgarian author’s preoccupation with stories and their power to upset life’s linear course. Like his idol Jorge Luis Borges, Gospodinov tends towards subversion in his fiction: he takes the “game” and rewrites the rules, turns the board upside down to find new ways of looking and seeing. If the ending is a foregone conclusion, Gospodinov’s magic is to make his stories feel like beginnings with endless possibilities.

The Man With Many Names comprises 40 stories made up of two collections previously published in Bulgarian. Ranging from post-Communist realism to experimental fables set in unfamiliar worlds, these magnificently imaginative pieces trade in many of the same themes – childhood, the labyrinthine qualities of language, the push and pull of fantasy and reality – as his best-known work, Time Shelter, for which he won the International Booker prize in 2023, shared with translator Angela Rodel, who also translated this collection. Here too Rodel expertly conveys Gospodinov’s economy of language, as well as his playfulness and warmth as a storyteller.

One of Gospodinov’s charming quirks is his tendency to speak directly to the reader, orienting them within the apparatus of the story. So let’s dive in, as he would say. One of the collection’s most affecting stories is Blind Vaysha (adapted into an Oscar-nominated animation by Theodore Ushev), the tale of a girl who with one eye sees into the future and with the other into the past. The trick is that Gospodinov turns Vaysha’s “blindness” into a more universal problem, as if to say we all see like Vaysha in some way.

Other standout stories in this fabular vein include The Christmas Soul of a Pig, in which a pig meditates on life, death, hypocrisy, and religion as he is prepped for slaughter; And Everything Became Moon, about a man who chooses the day of his death through a special government department; Eight Minutes and Nineteen Seconds, in which a world-renowned judge of sunsets returns to his home town to witness the apocalypse. In this story, we also bear witness to the molten core of Gospodinov’s outward morbidity; the sun has gone out, we have eight minutes to live, so what else is there to do but admire the beauty of a sunset?

Another persistent theme of the collection is love-that-cannot-be: missed connections, unfulfilled reunions. In Peonies and Forget-Me-Nots, one of the collection’s best stories, two strangers meet at an airport and fall in love. They accept they cannot be together, so invent a life of shared memories instead. After they part, the man returns home to his wife and can’t explain “what he’d been doing during those 50 years when he’d been gone” – as if their little game had bent the laws of time. Part of the pleasure of reading Gospodinov is the force of his imagination, which feels as insistently real as a child’s. This story mirrors Oh, Henry!, where two young lovers travel to each other’s home towns on Christmas Eve as a surprise, only to realise they both, tragically, had the same idea.

This twist on O Henry’s 1905 classic The Gift of the Magi is one of many literary hints that Gospodinov drops. There are stories that recall the psychological noir of Paul Auster, the literary gamesmanship of Vladimir Nabokov and the political acerbism of Milan Kundera (all three are referenced in the collection). And saturating everything he writes, the inventiveness of Borges. In the afterword, Gospodinov modestly describes “Borges and my grandmother” as his two key influences.

But Gospodinov’s world-building also has its own private logic, and in these stories we wade through the flotsam of his familiar inventory: trains (in A Second Story, A Station Story, Christine Waving from the Train and Daughter), ears and their potential dismemberment (in Forging the Bulgarian Earring, In Front of Hotel Bulgaria, and Six Degrees of Separation), the figure of the Minotaur (in The Eighth Night), cinema, Russian literature, flowers, pickles, ghosts, and dreary editorial offices. One final word must go to Gaustine, an elusive, shapeshifting character who is never far from view in Gospodinov’s works; readers may remember him as the psychiatrist in Time Shelter, and he appears in several of these stories. It is to him we are indebted for the idea above that “stories will always put off the end”, Gospodinov reveals, as well as other witty and wise interjections throughout. Hats off to Gaustine, and hats off to Gospodinov for telling us these stories while we postpone the ending.

entries.title: M John Harrison becomes first science fiction author to win the Booker prize
entries.summary: The 81-year-old’s postapocalyptic novel The End of Everything takes home the £50,000 awardGuardian fiction editor Justine Jordan on M John Harrison’s win: A visionary writer gets the recognition he deservesEighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history
entries.content:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.

Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.

Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.

The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.

Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”

Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.

This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.

Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.

His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”

Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.

The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.

The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

  • The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Jarvis Cocker on judging the Booker prize: ‘It’s just like being in a band’
entries.summary: The singer on how being in Pulp prepared him for judging a literary prize, reading 163 books while on tour, and feeling like the odd one out on the panel• M John Harrison becomes the first science fiction author to win the Booker prizeJudging the Booker prize is like being in a band. A band will often bring together a very disparate set of people, their only thing in common the fact they’re in the
entries.content:
Judging the Booker prize is like being in a band. A band will often bring together a very disparate set of people, their only thing in common the fact they’re in the same group. And a good band takes account of the interests and strengths of its members – that’s how you get a unique sound. Being part of this year’s Booker prize judging panel – chaired by Mary Beard, and featuring the writers Patricia Lockwood, Raymond Antrobus and Rebecca Liu – felt much the same. We were all very different, but we had a common cause: to pick a good winner.

Both bands and Booker prize panels are, at least ostensibly, democracies (though in Pulp, I’m the singer, so I make more noise than everybody else). But they shouldn’t be bland democracies. Mary didn’t expect us to toe a party line, and our panel managed to avoid what can sometimes happen when you’re on a jury and you end up agreeing on the least offensive option.

Walking into the final judging meeting last Saturday, I had three books in mind that I would have been happy to see win, but I had no idea who we’d land on. We seesawed around quite a lot, and it took a while, but we eventually managed to settle on a winner. And no scones were thrown at each other in the process.

We agreed that The End of Everything by M John Harrison is not a particularly easy book to read. But that’s not because it’s badly written – it’s actually very well written. The author is telling us that the thing that has gone wrong with the world is something that no one can really understand. For too many readers, Harrison has flown under the radar – this book is a culmination of his craft.

I judged the Booker prize while touring – the 163 eligible novels helped fill long, usually very boring flights. I couldn’t lug around a massive bag of books, so I had to read them on my iPad. I wouldn’t recommend it as a reading experience, but in this case it did help me be fairly objective – I couldn’t be put off by a rubbish cover. I also wasn’t aware of the author’s name when I was reading a book, meaning any conscious or unconscious prejudices that I may have had towards them disappeared. I sometimes had to do a judging meeting while on tour – when in Sydney, the time difference meant one of the sessions ran from 1am to 3am (luckily it wasn’t the night we played).

I ended up reading The End of Everything three times. During the re-reading process, some of the books deepened – you saw bits that you missed on the first read – and others shallowed out – you felt like you’d got everything the first time round.

Going into the process, I was worried it would put me off reading. I also felt, rightly or wrongly, like I was the least qualified judge – the odd one out on a panel of established writers and industry professionals. So in some ways I’m surprised I enjoyed it so much. I’m definitely never going to read 163 books in a year again, but I’ve certainly become a faster reader – I now finish a book in three or four days (though I don’t know if that’ll last, or if I’ll slow down to my usual tortoiselike pace again). And I’ve discovered contemporary writers I love, who I’ll continue to follow.

I’d never been in a book club before this; reading had always been a solitary pursuit. But in the way that reading a book is sometimes a welcome relief from your own consciousness, listening to what the other judges, with different modes of life, had to say about the books was fascinating. Anyone who’s invited to be a Booker prize judge is in for a treat.

entries.title: Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan Coe review – what can music tell us about national identity?

In 1907, composer Ralph Vaughan Williams confided to the critic Edwin Evans that he was finding his own music “lumpy and stodgy”. His musical education at the Royal College of Music, and indeed classical music in England in general at that time, had tended towards the Teutonic – Bach, Brahms, Beethoven, Wagner – and their heavy contrapuntal style dominated his work. To free himself, he told Evans, he planned to spend some months studying under French composer Vincent d’Indy, who taught at the Paris Conservatoire. Evans’s colleague, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi, had other ideas. He proposed that, rather than the traditionalist d’Indy, Vaughan Williams should take lessons with his close friend Maurice Ravel, by then one of the most admired young composers in France.

The two men could hardly have been more different: Ravel petite, fastidious, intensely private, an avid collector of intricate mechanical toys; Vaughan Williams bulky, dishevelled, bluffly nonconformist, and possessed of a fascination for English folk music that Ravel found incomprehensible. But though they got off to a poor start (in their first lesson Ravel set Vaughan Williams to compose a little minuet in the style of Mozart, an exercise the Englishman refused in no uncertain terms to consider), the three months they spent together in Paris marked the start of a friendship that would profoundly touch both men and their music.

In a recent interview, Jonathan Coe admitted that “ever since I discovered that my two favourite composers … were friends and supporters of each other, I’ve wanted to write a novel about them”. Their music clearly delights him – the book comes with a splendid playlist – but what surely made this story irresistible to Coe, that great chronicler of Englishness, was how both Vaughan Williams and Ravel came, in their work, to embody something quintessential about their respective countries. Widely celebrated for its clarity, elegance and formal emotional control, Ravel’s music exemplifies the pinnacle of French cultural values, while Vaughan Williams drew on ancient hymns, chorales and folk music to create work in a consciously English tradition. “‘Englishry’ is in the very blood and bones of his music,” the Times declared in 1952, an assessment supported by Ravel, who described his friend as “a real artist, who only realised his richness when he learned to be English!”

Lessons in Harmony takes the form of an unpublished memoir written by Ravel’s devoted friend Pierre “Mylo” Mylonas, loosely based on Calvocoressi, after Ravel’s death, and “discovered” accidentally decades later. Coe, himself an accomplished musician, has described the book as a fantasia, a freeform composition that does not follow strict traditional structures, and the novel has all of the exhilarating immediacy of improvisation, shifting suddenly in tempo and mood, modulating frequently to unexpected keys. An inserted section written by another of Ravel’s pupils about a visit to London that Mylo had to miss is interpolated with Mylo’s exasperated corrections, while a virtuoso vignette involving the shifting of a piano might have come straight from Buster Keaton.

Lessons in Harmony is the story of an unlikely and transformative friendship. It is also a masterful examination of national identity and how it shapes us. Mylo, born to a Portuguese father and Greek mother, shuttling between London and Paris, is a man without a homeland, an often penniless polyglot moored by a single fixed point: his private passion for Ravel. Beneath the surface of his beguilingly partisan account lies a mesh of conflicting dualities: of nature and artifice, tradition and modernity, slapstick and seriousness, egoism and generosity of spirit, selfhood and country. Ravel and Vaughan Williams may remain as chalk and cheese but, as the understanding between them deepens, and works its way into their music, the lines between them soften and blur. Mylo himself is altered by the changes in them – opened up. It is only with the advent of the first world war, with national identity hardened and pressed into the service of mass slaughter, that the connection stutters, redrawing borders and forcing a retreat.

Ravel and Vaughan Williams both served in that terrible conflict, Ravel in the trenches and Vaughan Williams as an ambulance driver. They fought on the same side, facing the same enemy, but, though they remained in touch, their friendship never quite recovered. Two decades later the world was at war once again. In the opening pages of Coe’s subtly tender and generous novel, Vaughan Williams asks his friend Evans if he thinks it is possible for music to represent the soul of a nation. At its close, as Mylo recalls the triumphant premiere of his Fifth Symphony at the Proms of 1943, the opinion of the critics is a resounding yes. In the darkness of war, Vaughan Williams stands as a beacon of hope, an expression of a deep shared Englishness, an inspiration and a benediction. Whether great music can ever be that simply categorised, and whether indeed we who listen to it can hope to live up to so noble an ideal of nationhood, Coe leaves it to us to judge.
